title: Azielon PMP Topic Notes
purpose: Source-grounded topic notes organized by People, Process, and Business Environment for later app integration.

topics.title: Servant Leadership & PM Mindset
topics.summary: Lead by enabling the team rather than controlling every task. The uploaded People notes emphasize coaching, removing blockers, empowering the team, protecting focus, active listening, and adapting leadership to the situation.
keyRules: Coach and mentor rather than micromanage.
Remove impediments and enable team decisions.
Talk directly with people before escalating when appropriate.
Adapt leadership style to team maturity and context.
Model transparency, respect, accountability, and psychological safety.
topics.doFirst: Understand the team member's need or obstacle, then coach or remove the impediment before escalating.
examTraps: Defaulting to command-and-control with a capable team.
Escalating a team issue before trying direct collaboration.
Solving every team problem personally instead of enabling the team.
topics.flowOrMemory: Understand → Listen → Coach/Enable → Remove blocker → Monitor → Escalate if needed

topics.title: Conflict Resolution
topics.summary: The uploaded leadership material presents the Thomas-Kilmann modes and frames collaborate/problem solve as the generally preferred win-win approach, while force/direct is reserved for urgent or non-negotiable contexts.
keyRules: Collaborate/problem solve seeks a durable win-win solution.
Compromise means both sides give up something.
Smooth/accommodate emphasizes agreement but may not solve root cause.
Force/direct is for urgent, safety-critical, or non-negotiable situations.
Withdraw/avoid is limited and temporary.
topics.doFirst: Understand the conflict and underlying interests before choosing a response style.
examTraps: Treating compromise as the same as collaboration.
Assuming personality is the root cause before assessing schedule, priorities, resources, or technical issues.
Escalating before direct resolution is attempted.
topics.flowOrMemory: Listen → Identify root cause → Collaborate → Agree action → Monitor

topics.title: Team Development — Tuckman
topics.summary: Team development is presented as Forming → Storming → Norming → Performing → Adjourning. Storming is normal, teams can regress, and leadership should change as the team matures.
keyRules: Forming needs clarity and direction.
Storming includes normal conflict over roles and approach.
Norming develops working agreements.
Performing brings high autonomy and performance.
Adjourning closes the team experience and captures learning.
Team changes can cause regression to an earlier stage.
topics.doFirst: Identify the team's current stage before deciding how much direction, coaching, or delegation is appropriate.
examTraps: Trying to skip Storming entirely.
Replacing people too early when normal team development is occurring.
Using the same leadership style at every stage.
topics.flowOrMemory: Forming → Storming → Norming → Performing → Adjourning

topics.title: Motivation Theories
topics.summary: The People notes cover Maslow, Herzberg, McGregor X/Y, McClelland, Vroom, Ouchi, and situational leadership. The goal is recognizing what motivates behavior rather than memorizing names alone.
keyRules: Maslow progresses from physiological needs through safety, belonging, esteem, and self-actualization.
Herzberg separates hygiene factors from motivators.
McGregor contrasts Theory X control assumptions with Theory Y self-motivation.
McClelland focuses on achievement, affiliation, and power.
Vroom links effort → performance → valued reward.
topics.doFirst: Identify the underlying human need or motivation problem before selecting a leadership response.
examTraps: Using compensation as the answer to every motivation problem.
Ignoring team maturity or human needs.
Treating motivation models as rigid formulas.
topics.flowOrMemory: Need → Motivation signal → Appropriate leadership response

topics.title: Stakeholder Identification & Engagement
topics.summary: Stakeholder work is not a one-time list. The uploaded materials emphasize early identification, analysis of power/interest and engagement, tailored communication, and continuous monitoring.
keyRules: Identify stakeholders early and continuously.
Analyze interest, influence, power, expectations, and engagement.
Tailor engagement and communication rather than using one method for everyone.
Update stakeholder information as relationships change.
Understand resistance before choosing an engagement strategy.
topics.doFirst: Identify/analyze the stakeholder's position and cause of resistance before selecting an engagement action.
examTraps: Sending more communication without understanding resistance.
Treating the stakeholder register as static.
Escalating resistance without analysis.
topics.flowOrMemory: Identify → Analyze → Engage → Monitor

topics.title: Communication
topics.summary: Communication notes emphasize tailoring method and frequency to stakeholder needs, active listening, and correcting structural communication problems through the communications approach rather than reactive messaging.
keyRules: Tailor channel, frequency, detail, and format to stakeholder needs.
Use active listening: paraphrase, clarify, acknowledge, then solve.
Review communication arrangements when unofficial or ineffective information flows cause problems.
Distributed teams need deliberate information sharing and communication norms.
topics.doFirst: Understand why communication is failing and who needs what information before adding more messages or meetings.
trickyDistinctions: Communication plan vs stakeholder engagement plan
Push vs pull vs interactive communication
examTraps: Assuming more communication automatically fixes the problem.
Using one channel for every stakeholder.
Punitive memos instead of fixing the communication process.
topics.flowOrMemory: Audience → Need → Method → Frequency → Feedback → Adjust

topics.title: Roles, Authority & Influence
topics.summary: The leadership and roles materials distinguish formal authority from influence. The PM often works through expert and referent power, while decision rights depend on governance and delivery context.
keyRules: Expert power comes from knowledge and competence.
Referent power comes from respect and relationships.
Legitimate power comes from formal organizational position.
Coercive power is a last resort.
Role authority differs across sponsor, PM, functional manager, Product Owner, Scrum Master, and team.
topics.doFirst: Determine who owns the decision and act at the lowest appropriate authority level before escalating.
examTraps: Assuming the PM owns every decision.
Using escalation as a substitute for influence.
Confusing backlog priority authority with task assignment authority.
topics.flowOrMemory: Problem → Check role/authority → Engage owner → Act → Escalate if authority gap remains

topics.title: Coaching & Team Performance
topics.summary: Coaching is used to improve capability and performance without taking ownership away from the team. The uploaded materials emphasize feedback, psychological safety, mentoring, and helping teams improve their own process.
keyRules: Coach before replacing people when development can solve the problem.
Use private, direct conversations for individual behavior concerns.
Retrospectives are the forum for agile process improvement.
Encourage cross-skilling and knowledge transfer when continuity is at risk.
topics.doFirst: Observe and understand the performance gap, then coach privately or facilitate team improvement before punitive action.
examTraps: Publicly criticizing an individual.
Replacing a person before understanding root cause.
Taking over the team's work.
topics.flowOrMemory: Observe → Understand → Coach → Agree improvement → Follow up

topics.title: Agile Team Roles & Ceremonies
topics.summary: The lifecycle notes distinguish Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers, Sprint Review, Retrospective, and Daily Scrum. Review concerns the product and stakeholders; retrospective concerns the team's process.
keyRules: Product Owner owns value and backlog ordering.
Developers decide how to do the work and manage the Sprint plan.
Scrum Master facilitates, coaches, and removes impediments.
Sprint Review inspects product/increment with stakeholders.
Retrospective inspects team process and improvement.
Daily Scrum is not a management status meeting.
topics.doFirst: Identify whether the question is about product/value, team process, impediments, or work execution before choosing the role/event.
examTraps: Using the Daily Scrum as a status meeting.
Putting stakeholders into the retrospective as decision makers.
Having a PM assign every daily task in a self-managing team.
topics.flowOrMemory: Value/Backlog → Sprint Planning → Sprint/Sync → Increment → Review → Retrospective

topics.title: Integration & Project Flow
topics.summary: The foundations and flow materials emphasize integration: the PM connects scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, risk, stakeholders, procurement, and value instead of optimizing one area in isolation.
keyRules: Integrate decisions across project areas.
Assess cross-impact before making changes.
Keep plans aligned after approved changes.
Use data to understand performance before acting.
Optimize overall project value rather than one department's local objective.
topics.doFirst: Understand the impact across the project before selecting a local fix.
trickyDistinctions: Project management plan vs subsidiary plans
examTraps: Fixing schedule at the expense of quality/value.
Changing one plan while leaving related plans inconsistent.
topics.flowOrMemory: Data → Analyze → Insight → Decision → Action → Monitor

topics.title: Scope & Requirements
topics.summary: Scope notes distinguish requirements, acceptance criteria, RTM, scope statement, WBS, WBS dictionary, and formal handling of requested changes.
keyRules: Requirements express stakeholder/product needs.
RTM traces requirements through delivery, verification, and acceptance.
WBS decomposes project scope; WBS Dictionary adds detail.
Approved scope baselines are controlled references.
New scope in predictive work requires analysis and the defined change process.
topics.doFirst: Clarify the request and assess whether it is already approved scope, a missed requirement, or a new change.
examTraps: Adding work informally because it sounds reasonable.
Updating the baseline before approval.
Confusing traceability with decomposition.
topics.flowOrMemory: Need → Requirement → Acceptance Criteria → Scope/WBS → Deliver → Verify → Accept

topics.title: Schedule & Network Logic
topics.summary: Schedule learning should connect activity logic, dependencies, float, critical path, and compression trade-offs rather than treating formulas as isolated facts.
keyRules: Critical path determines the longest path through the network and generally drives project duration.
Total float concerns delay without delaying project finish; free float concerns delay without delaying the next activity.
Fast tracking overlaps work and raises rework/risk.
Crashing adds resources/cost to shorten critical-path work.
Resource leveling may extend schedule; smoothing uses available float.
topics.doFirst: Identify the schedule constraint or path causing the problem before choosing a compression or resource action.
examTraps: Compressing noncritical work to solve a critical-path delay.
Assuming all schedule compression has the same cost/risk effect.
topics.flowOrMemory: Activities → Dependencies → Network → Critical Path/Float → Optimize → Monitor

topics.title: Cost, EVM & Forecasting
topics.summary: The EVM material teaches the story first: Plan it → Earn it → Spend it → Forecast it. PV, EV, and AC unlock the formulas, followed by variance/index and EAC/ETC/VAC interpretation.
keyRules: PV = budgeted value of work that should be done.
EV = budgeted value of work actually completed.
AC = actual money spent.
CPI = EV/AC and SPI = EV/PV.
EAC forecasts total expected final cost; ETC is remaining expected cost.
Use formula assumptions deliberately rather than mechanically.
topics.doFirst: Determine what the numbers mean operationally before selecting a management response.
examTraps: Treating SV as elapsed time.
Using a formula without checking its assumption.
Confusing cost baseline with project budget.
topics.flowOrMemory: Plan it → Earn it → Spend it → Forecast it

topics.title: Quality & Acceptance
topics.summary: The quality materials frame quality as conformance + fitness for use, with prevention over inspection. They distinguish Manage Quality, Control Quality, and formal acceptance.
keyRules: Build quality into the process rather than relying only on inspection.
Manage Quality is process/execution focused.
Control Quality measures/inspects results for conformance.
Validate Scope obtains formal acceptance from the authorized stakeholder.
A verified deliverable is not yet necessarily accepted.
topics.doFirst: Determine whether the problem is process quality, product conformance, or stakeholder acceptance before acting.
examTraps: Assuming internal testing equals customer acceptance.
Treating quality as final inspection only.
Gold plating under the label of quality.
topics.flowOrMemory: Need → Acceptance Criteria → Build Quality In → Control Quality → Validate/Accept

topics.title: Risk & Issues
topics.summary: The Risk materials distinguish future uncertainty from current issues and organize work around identification, qualitative/quantitative analysis, responses, reserves, and monitoring.
keyRules: Risk is an uncertain future event/condition; an issue is a current problem.
Qualitative analysis prioritizes risks; quantitative analysis numerically models uncertainty.
Threat and opportunity responses differ.
When a risk occurs, it becomes a current issue and must be managed as such.
Risk monitoring continues throughout the project.
topics.doFirst: Ask whether the event is still uncertain or has already happened, then use the appropriate risk or issue path.
examTraps: Keeping an occurred risk only in the risk register.
Ignoring secondary risk created by a response.
Re-analyzing a current issue as though it were still hypothetical.
topics.flowOrMemory: Risk → Analyze → Respond → Monitor → Issue (if it occurs); Issue → Analyze → Resolve → Monitor

topics.title: Reserves & Risk Funding
topics.summary: Reserve notes distinguish contingency reserve from management reserve and connect funding decisions to identified vs unforeseen uncertainty.
keyRules: Contingency reserve supports identified risks/known-unknowns.
Management reserve supports unforeseen uncertainty/unknown-unknowns.
Management reserve sits outside the cost baseline.
Reserve use should follow the organization's authority/governance rules.
topics.doFirst: Identify whether the uncertainty was already known/identified before selecting a reserve or change action.
examTraps: Using management reserve for every overrun.
Treating reserve access as authority-free.
Using a reserve instead of addressing a necessary change.
topics.flowOrMemory: Identify uncertainty → Determine known/unknown → Use proper reserve/authority → Update records

topics.title: Procurement
topics.summary: The procurement cheat sheet emphasizes clear scope, right contract, fair selection, active monitoring, formal change, and clean closure.
keyRules: Define procurement need and scope clearly.
Choose contract type based on scope certainty and risk allocation.
Use approved source-selection criteria; lowest price is not automatically best.
Buyer creates solicitation documents; seller creates responses/proposals/quotes.
Negotiate/manage within the contract before unnecessary escalation.
Contract change and project change may both be needed if baselines are affected.
topics.doFirst: Check the contract/procurement documents and understand the issue before escalating or changing terms.
examTraps: Selecting solely on lowest price.
Confusing buyer solicitation with seller response.
Ignoring project change control when a contract change affects baselines.
topics.flowOrMemory: Need → Make/Buy → SOW → Solicit → Select → Award → Manage → Close

topics.title: Resources & Capacity
topics.summary: Resource questions often test negotiation, role authority, continuity, knowledge transfer, and the schedule effect of leveling/smoothing.
keyRules: Understand who owns the resource in the organization.
Negotiate directly with the functional/resource owner before escalation where appropriate.
Use knowledge transfer when a resource is leaving or being replaced.
Leveling may change the schedule; smoothing works within float.
topics.doFirst: Assess the impact and discuss the resource issue with the responsible owner before escalating.
trickyDistinctions: Knowledge transfer vs retaining a resource
PM authority vs functional manager authority
examTraps: Assuming the charter overrides the functional manager.
Escalating before negotiation.
Ignoring knowledge continuity during transition.
topics.flowOrMemory: Need/Conflict → Assess impact → Negotiate → Adjust/Transfer → Escalate if unresolved

topics.title: Documents & Artifacts
topics.summary: The document deck provides a compact memory system: WHY = Business Case; AUTHORITY = Charter/Governance; HOW = Management Plan; APPROVED = Baseline; MAY HAPPEN = Risk Register; HAPPENED = Issue Log; TRACE = RTM; DETAIL = WBS Dictionary; CHANGE STATUS = Change Log; SELLER = Contract.
keyRules: Management plans explain how work will be managed.
Baselines are approved performance references.
Registers/logs track evolving items.
Reports communicate analyzed information.
Living documents evolve; controlled baselines change only through authorized governance.
topics.doFirst: Identify what kind of artifact the scenario is asking for: why, authority, how, approved target, tracking, traceability, detail, status, or seller agreement.
examTraps: Updating the wrong artifact because names sound similar.
Treating a baseline as a freely editable plan.
Using a log as approval.
topics.flowOrMemory: WHY → Business Case | AUTHORITY → Charter | HOW → Plan | APPROVED → Baseline | TRACK → Register/Log

topics.title: Integrated Change Control
topics.summary: Change control material repeatedly emphasizes sequence: analyze impact before approval or implementation, follow the defined authority path, then update and communicate.
keyRules: Do not implement first and analyze later.
Assess impact before asking the approval authority to decide.
If controlled baselines are affected, use the formal change process.
Approved changes require updates to relevant plans/baselines/documents and communication.
Sponsor preference does not automatically bypass the approved process.
topics.doFirst: Understand the requested change and analyze its impact before implementation; then route it through the appropriate approval process.
examTraps: Going to the CCB before impact analysis is complete.
Implementing because the sponsor requested it.
Changing the baseline casually.
topics.flowOrMemory: Change identified → Impact analysis → Change request → Decision → Update/Communicate → Implement → Monitor

topics.title: Predictive, Iterative, Incremental, Agile & Hybrid
topics.summary: The lifecycle deck uses a memorable spectrum: Predictive = know it/plan it; Iterative = improve it; Incremental = add to it; Agile = learn/adapt; Hybrid = blend what fits.
keyRules: Choose the approach based on requirements stability, uncertainty, feedback, incremental value, and constraints.
Predictive uses planning, baselines, and controlled change.
Iterative refines repeated versions.
Incremental adds usable pieces.
Agile uses frequent feedback and adaptation.
Hybrid intentionally combines approaches for different needs.
topics.doFirst: Identify the work's uncertainty, delivery needs, stakeholder feedback, and constraints before choosing the approach.
trickyDistinctions: Predictive change control vs agile backlog change
examTraps: Picking Agile because it sounds modern.
Treating hybrid as random mixing.
Assuming predictive means no change or Agile means no planning.
topics.flowOrMemory: Stable → Predictive | Refine → Iterative | Add pieces → Incremental | Evolving → Agile | Mixed → Hybrid

topics.title: Scrum & Kanban
topics.summary: The lifecycle notes distinguish Scrum cadence from Kanban flow. Scrum uses sprints and defined accountabilities/events; Kanban visualizes flow, limits WIP, and measures throughput/cycle time.
keyRules: Scrum = cadence, Sprint events, backlog ordering, velocity context.
Kanban = continuous flow, WIP limits, pull, throughput/cycle time.
A visual board alone does not make a process Kanban.
When WIP is exceeded, investigate the bottleneck and help work finish.
topics.doFirst: Determine whether the scenario is about cadence/roles/events or flow/WIP/bottlenecks.
examTraps: Using velocity as a Kanban metric.
Starting more work when WIP is already exceeded.
Assuming every board is Kanban.
topics.flowOrMemory: Scrum: Plan → Sprint → Review → Retro | Kanban: Visualize → Limit WIP → Pull → Measure flow → Improve

topics.title: Governance & Decision Authority
topics.summary: Governance tells you who has authority to decide what. The uploaded Business Environment notes use the flow Problem → Assess → Check → Owner → Act → Escalate.
keyRules: The PM manages within delegated authority; not every decision belongs to the PM.
Check governance/decision rights before acting on major strategic or controlled decisions.
Use the lowest responsible authority level that can resolve the issue.
Urgency does not automatically justify bypassing governance.
topics.doFirst: Assess the issue and identify the decision owner/authority before acting or escalating.
examTraps: PM makes a major strategic decision alone.
Bypassing governance because action is urgent.
Escalating before analyzing.
topics.flowOrMemory: Problem → Assess → Check authority → Owner → Act → Escalate if needed

topics.title: Compliance
topics.summary: Compliance material treats laws, regulations, safety, audit, policy, and mandatory requirements as non-optional constraints that cannot simply be traded away for schedule or cost.
keyRules: Identify the compliance requirement and assess project impact.
Consult relevant compliance/legal/safety expertise where needed.
Follow mandatory rules and the appropriate governance/change process.
Document corrective actions and prevent recurrence.
topics.doFirst: Identify and assess the compliance gap, then consult the right expert/authority before implementing the response.
examTraps: Ignoring compliance because scope is baselined.
Choosing speed over legal/safety requirements.
Treating mandatory controls as negotiable.
topics.flowOrMemory: Identify → Assess → Consult → Update → Implement → Document

topics.title: Organizational Change & Adoption
topics.summary: The Business Environment notes explicitly separate organizational change from project change: organizational change is about people adopting a new behavior/capability, not just baseline control.
keyRules: Understand the cause of resistance.
Engage affected stakeholders.
Communicate benefits and reasons for change.
Train and enable users.
Reinforce adoption and monitor uptake.
topics.doFirst: Understand why people are resisting and engage them before forcing adoption or escalating.
examTraps: Treating resistance as defiance to punish.
Using change control as the answer to a people-adoption problem.
Assuming deployment equals adoption.
topics.flowOrMemory: Understand → Engage → Communicate → Train → Reinforce

topics.title: Benefits & Value Realization
topics.summary: The value materials emphasize Deliverable → Outcome → Benefit → Value and warn that completed scope is not the same as realized business value.
keyRules: A deliverable is not automatically a benefit.
Benefits should be measurable.
Benefits may continue after project closure.
Operational/business owners may continue tracking benefits after handoff.
Use stakeholder feedback and outcome metrics to reassess value.
topics.doFirst: Ask what business outcome/value was intended and how it will be measured before declaring success.
trickyDistinctions: Output vs outcome vs benefit vs value
examTraps: Assuming on-time/on-budget equals success.
Treating handoff as the end of value.
Using ROI alone as the only business-value metric.
topics.flowOrMemory: Deliverable → Outcome → Benefit → Strategic Value → Measure/Owner

topics.title: Strategic Alignment & Business Case
topics.summary: Foundations and value-delivery material distinguish business need, business case, project delivery, benefits, and strategic value.
keyRules: Business need explains the problem/opportunity.
Business case justifies why the investment should proceed.
Projects should remain aligned with organizational strategy.
If value or strategy changes materially, reassess rather than continue automatically.
topics.doFirst: Reassess the business case/strategic alignment when market, regulatory, competitor, or strategy conditions materially change.
examTraps: Continuing because the project was once approved.
Confusing delivery success with strategic value.
Selecting projects by one metric only.
topics.flowOrMemory: Business Need → Business Case → Project → Benefits → Value

topics.title: Responsible AI & Sustainability
topics.summary: The Business Environment material frames AI as decision support with human accountability and sustainability as environmental + social + economic lifecycle thinking.
keyRules: Validate AI data, assumptions, and output before acting.
Protect privacy/security and do not upload sensitive data without approval.
Humans remain accountable for governance decisions.
Sustainability considers environmental, social, and economic effects.
Optimize lifecycle value rather than lowest upfront price or fastest schedule alone.
topics.doFirst: For AI: validate data/assumptions/output before deciding. For sustainability: assess lifecycle impacts and criteria before choosing an option.
trickyDistinctions: Purchase price vs total lifecycle value
examTraps: Treating AI output as final authority.
Ignoring privacy/security because AI is convenient.
Choosing cheapest/fastest without lifecycle impact.
topics.flowOrMemory: AI: Data OK? → Privacy? → Generate → Validate → Decide | Sustainability: Impact → Alternatives → Criteria → Balance → Monitor

topics.title: Finance & Project Selection
topics.summary: The Finance and Business Environment formula notes frame formulas as decision support: calculate, interpret, validate, decide.
keyRules: ROI compares return relative to cost.
BCR compares benefits to costs.
Payback estimates time to recover investment.
NPV expresses value in present-value terms.
IRR is a rate-of-return concept.
Opportunity cost is the best alternative forgone.
Sunk cost is already spent and should not drive forward decisions.
Evaluate lifecycle cost/TCO rather than purchase price alone.
topics.doFirst: Calculate the relevant metric, interpret what it means, then validate against strategy, risk, compliance, adoption, and lifecycle impact.
examTraps: Choosing the mathematically highest metric while ignoring compliance or strategy.
Continuing because of sunk cost.
Choosing lowest purchase price instead of lifecycle value.
topics.flowOrMemory: Calculate → Interpret → Validate → Decide

topics.title: Project, Program, Portfolio & Operations
topics.summary: Foundations material distinguishes temporary project work from ongoing operations and separates project outcomes, program benefits, and portfolio strategy.
keyRules: Project = temporary initiative with defined beginning/end and unique outcome.
Operations = ongoing repetitive business work.
Program = related projects coordinated for combined benefits.
Portfolio = projects/programs/other work selected and managed for strategic alignment.
topics.doFirst: Identify whether the scenario's primary focus is a single outcome, related benefits, strategic selection, or ongoing operations.
examTraps: Assuming a long project is not temporary.
Treating a program as simply a large project.
Assuming portfolio components must all be directly related.
topics.flowOrMemory: Project → Outcome | Program → Benefits | Portfolio → Strategy | Operations → Run the business
